papers.title_in_file: Teaching quantum information technologies and a practical module for online and offline undergraduate students
papers.version_note: arXiv:2112.06548v1 [physics.ed-ph], 13 Dec 2021. Text layer holds the paper once, 8 pages. Tables I and II and the figure labels come through as fragments; Table II is read from its fragments.
papers.what_it_is: A course-experience letter from Shanghai Jiao Tong University describing a 12-week undergraduate quantum computing course, its 1-credit team project module, and its online and offline blended classroom.

assertions.value: The authors state that the course includes a 3-credit teaching course and a 1-credit practical module.
quotes: This course includes a 3-credit teaching course and a 1-credit practical module.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the structure of their own course in the Introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that the teaching part of the course lasts 12 weeks, with each week having teaching time of 4×45 minutes.
quotes: The teaching for this course lasts 12 weeks, and each week has teaching time lasting 4×45 minutes
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the schedule of their own course.

assertions.value: The authors state that the course covers quantum computing hardware, algorithms and applications, with a basic introduction to quantum communication and quantum metrology, and that its approaches include universal digital, analog and hybrid quantum-classical variational quantum computing.
quotes: We develop a holistic curriculum for quantum computing covering the quantum computing hardware, quantum computing algorithms and applications, as well as a basic introduction on quantum communication and quantum metrology.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the scope of their own curriculum in the Introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that the grade for the teaching course has three parts: in-class performance and homework (30%), the oral talk (35%) and the final-term exam (35%).
quotes: the in-class performance and homework (30%), the oral talk (35%) and the ﬁnal-term exam (35%)
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the grading rule of their own course.

assertions.value: The authors report that students in the past two rounds of the course came from a wide range of majors, including physics, mathematics, computer science, software, electronics, information security and telecommunication.
quotes: the students who have selected our course in the past two rounds are majored in physics, mathematics, computer science, software, electronics, information security, telecommunication
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors describe the enrolled cohort of their own course; no enrollment counts are given.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no enrollment numbers, so the breadth of majors is not weighted by headcount.

assertions.value: The authors state that they teach Grover algorithm, quantum annealing, VQE and QAOA, and show students how to apply each of these quantum algorithms to the same quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) task, so that students can judge how to select an algorithm for a given task.
quotes: we shall teach Grover algorithm, quantum annealing, Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE)[14], and Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)[15]
and show to students how to apply each of these
quantum algorithms on the same quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) task.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the design of their own curriculum.

assertions.value: The authors claim that online learning resources for quantum computing are segmented and not systematic, and that tutorials from commercial companies might focus on the approach used by that company, for example D-Wave on quantum annealing and IBM Qiskit on circuit-based quantum computing.
quotes: They are segmented and not that systematic.
The tutorials provided by commercial companies might focus on the quantum computing approach used in their own companies.
D-Wave[12] teaches quantum annealing, while IBM Qiskit[13] tutorial mainly covers circuit-based quantum computing.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; the paper gives no survey of the resources.
assertions.reader_inference: The motivation for a platform-neutral curriculum rests on this unsurveyed claim.

assertions.value: The authors state that the two textbooks they recommend (Nielsen and Chuang; Benenti, Casati and Strini) were first published in 2000 and 2004, and claim this means they have almost missed the quick development stage of quantum computing in the past two decades.
quotes: published in 2000 and 2004, respectively.
This means they have almost missed the quickly development stage for quantum computing in the past two decades.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim about the age of textbooks; the paper's reference list gives a 2010 edition for one of them.
assertions.reader_inference: Reference 9 in the paper is the 2010 anniversary edition, so the 2000 date is for the first edition only.

assertions.value: The authors state that of the two textbooks they recommend, the Benenti, Casati and Strini book is the more accessible, written for undergraduate students in physics, mathematics and computer sciences, and that they recommend both books to the class, especially the second.
quotes: written for undergraduate students in physics, mathematics and computer sciences
We recommend both books to students in our class, especially the second one
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's judgment of textbook accessibility.

assertions.value: The authors claim that adiabatic quantum computing and hybrid quantum-classical variational quantum computing are now being extensively researched as an alternative to universal quantum computing, and find many quantum advantages in various applications. The paper gives no citation or evidence for this statement.
quotes: are now being extensively researched as an alternative to universal quantum computing
many quantum advantages in various appplications.
assertions.certainty_reason: An unreferenced author claim.
assertions.reader_inference: The claim of many quantum advantages is broad and not backed in the paper; treat it as the authors' motivation, not as evidence.

assertions.value: The authors state that linear algebra with matrix calculation is the method they mainly use, without heavy quantum mechanics or classical computation terminology, and that they highlight three sets of tools: the underlying physics and hardware, analytic tools such as matrix or Dirac notation, and geometric tools such as the Bloch sphere and the angles between vectors used to understand Grover search.
quotes: Especially, linear algebra with matrix calculation is the method we mainly use
the geometric tool such as the Bloch sphere and the angles between vectors used for understanding the Grover search
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the method of their own course.

assertions.value: The authors state that QAOA is an adapted adiabatic optimization algorithm that can be implemented in universal quantum circuits and is essentially inspired by adiabatic quantum computing (AQC), and so AQC is taught as prior knowledge for QAOA.
quotes: QAOA, as an adapted adiabatic optimization algorithm that can be implemented in universal quantum circuits, is essentially inspired from AQC.
Therefore, AQC sets as the prior knowledge for studying QAOA.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of the authors in a teaching context, without derivation in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the stated reason for the teaching order (annealing and AQC before VQE and QAOA).

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum annealing or adiabatic quantum computing can be viewed as an analog quantum evolution similar to quantum walk, but with a time-dependent Hamiltonian.
quotes: can be viewed as an analog quantum evolution similar to quantum walk, but with a time-dependent Hamiltonian.
assertions.certainty_reason: A teaching-level characterization stated without derivation.

assertions.value: The authors state that variational quantum computing such as VQE and QAOA inspires the concept and method of the parameterized quantum circuit (PQC), which is widely used for quantum machine learning, and that this motivates the order of the sessions on quantum optimization and then quantum machine learning with a quantum feature map using PQC.
quotes: variational quantum computing like VQE and QAOA inspires the concept and method of parameterized quantum circuit (PQC)[23], which is then widely used for quantum machine learning.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's statement, with a citation to other work.

assertions.value: The authors describe Boson sampling as a very popular task to show impressive quantum advantage, with Gaussian Boson sampling as a further useful variation, and state that teaching multi-particle quantum walks makes these easier for students to understand.
quotes: Boson sampling[19], a very popular task to show impressive quantum advantage
show diﬀerent behaviors of fermions, bosons and indistinguishable particles
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result and an author's teaching claim.

assertions.value: The authors state that oral talks extend the curriculum with student contributions by interest and strength and relieve the discrepancy of students' prior knowledge, and that they announce two or three topics in every class instead of listing all topics at once.
assertions.anchor: Curriculum development, p.4; Table I, p.3
quotes: the setting of oral talks also helps to relieve the discrepancy of students’ prior knowledge
we do not list all oral talk topics at once, but announce two or three topics in every class
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's account of the benefit of a teaching method; no student outcome data are given.
assertions.reader_inference: No measured learning outcome supports the stated benefit.

assertions.value: The authors state that Table I oral talk topics serve three goals: Goal I emphasizes hardware and physics for quantum devices; Goal II is for students to digest news and analyze it with quantum knowledge; Goal III encourages students to go deeper than textbooks and explore frontier fields. Topics in the table include quantum machine learning topics such as QGAN and quantum reinforcement learning.
quotes: Goal I: We emphasize hardware and physics for quantum devices.
Goal II: We hope students can digest news and analyze it with quantum knowledge.
QGAN and its application
assertions.certainty_reason: The table note states the design of the authors' own oral talk topics.

assertions.value: The authors state that they mainly use Amazon Braket as the cloud platform because it has broad access to quantum annealers, universal quantum computers and classical computing resources; that they use their own software FeynmanPAQS as a photonic analog quantum simulator for analog quantum computing; and that they use the framework DeepQuantum, developed by a startup TuringQ, for quantum machine learning.
quotes: we mainly use Amazon Braket as it has broad access to quantum annealers, universal quantum computers and classical computing resources.
we use the software FeynmanPAQS[24] that we develop ourselves as a photonic analog quantum simulator
we use the framework DeepQuantum developed by a startup TuringQ.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the tools of their own course.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors are developers of FeynmanPAQS, so that tool choice is a self-use.

assertions.value: The authors state that after each quantum algorithm students set it up on a quantum computing platform, starting with the graphic interface at IBM Qiskit for students with little coding experience and later moving to Jupyter notebooks, including for quantum annealing on D-Wave hardware.
quotes: the students are asked to set up the quantum algorithm on their own in a quantum computing platform.
we use the graphic interface at IBM Qiskit (see Fig.2a)
operating quantum annealing on D-Wave hardware (see Fig.2b)
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the practice of their own course.

assertions.value: The authors state that teaching assistants are expected to know quantum computing well and be familiar with programming, prepare the Jupyter notebooks for algorithms and case studies, and answer student questions on operating the programs together with the teacher.
quotes: They are expected to be those who know quantum computing well themselves, and are familiar with programming.
The teaching assistant would prepare the Jupyter notebooks for quantum algorithms or case studies that will be used in class.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the staffing design of their own course.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the quantum optimization session they show how to map real-life optimization problems such as Max-cut, vertex cover, knapsack, graph partitioning and maximal independent set into a QUBO Hamiltonian and solve it with quantum algorithms.
quotes: we show how to map various real-life optimization problems such as Max-cut, vertex cover, knapsack, graph partitioning and maximal inde-
pendent set into a QUBO Hamiltonian and then solve it using quantum algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the content of their own session.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum machine learning session takes the quantum support vector machine (QSVM) as an example, shows the original swap-gate method for an inner product of quantum states, then shows that a quantum feature map made from parameterized quantum circuits can also form a QSVM, and covers data encoding, quantum feature maps and the parameter shift rule as a preferred method for gradient descent in quantum circuits.
quotes: we show the original method of using a swap gate to create an inner product of the quantum state
the quantum feature map made from parameterized quantum circuits can also be used to form a QSVM[26]
the parameter shift rule[27] as a preferred method for gradient descent in quantum circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the content of their own session; the 'preferred method' wording is their teaching judgment.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Preferred method' for parameter-shift gradients is an author preference, not a comparison made in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that derivative pricing may need the quantum amplitude estimation algorithm, portfolio optimization may resort to quantum annealing, and stock market prediction may involve some quantum machine learning; and that molecular energy calculation, molecular docking and protein folding can be solved using VQE, Gaussian Boson sampling or quantum annealing.
quotes: derivative pricing may need quantum amplitude estimation algorithm, portfolio optimization may resort to quantum annealing, and stock market prediction may involve some quantum machine learning.
molecular energy calculation, molecular docking and protein folding can also be solved using VQE, Gaussian Boson sampling or quantum annealing.
assertions.certainty_reason: Teaching-level statements of possibility, with no result or citation in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The wording 'may need', 'may resort to' and 'can also be solved' states possibility only; the paper reports no result for these applications.

assertions.value: The authors state that the 1-credit practical module runs in Week 13 to Week 16 after the 3-credit course, that students form teams of three and solve a real problem using any quantum approach, and that topics are flexible and can be suggested by the students.
quotes: Then we come to the 1-credit practical module during Week 13 and 16 after the 3-credit teaching course.
The students are asked to form teams of three and solve a real problem using any quantum approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the format of their own module.

assertions.value: The authors state three common requirements for all teams: real input data is required, with no strict lower bound on data size; at least one quantum approach shall be demonstrated, and a comparison of quantum with classical approaches, or of two or more quantum approaches, is encouraged; and the report is to be written in LaTeX with well presented figures. They state that teams do not necessarily need to show quantum advantage over a classical method.
quotes: Firstly, real input data is required.
There is no strict lower bound for the data size.
Secondly, at least one quantum approach shall be demonstrated.
They do not necessarily show quantum advantage over classical method
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the requirements of their own module.
assertions.reader_inference: With no lower bound on data size and no advantage requirement, a project result is not evidence of quantum advantage.

assertions.value: The authors list in Table II some practical projects done by students and the quantum technique each required; the table pairs protein folding with quantum annealing/VQE, and also lists medical image classification, computer vision for phase matching, quantum frustration for spin liquid, reinforcement learning, and natural language processing for music. The table gives no results of these projects.
quotes: TABLE II: Some practical projects and required quantum techniques
Project topic Protein folding
Quantum technique Quantum annealing/VQE
assertions.certainty_reason: The table lists the topics of the authors' own course projects; the text layer holds the table as fragments, so the full pairing is read from the layout.
assertions.reader_inference: The table reports project topics and techniques only; no accuracy, speed or advantage result is given for any project.

assertions.value: The authors state that each practical class has three parts: student progress reports, expert tips from researchers or engineers in fields such as quantum computing for ETF trading, drug design or computer vision, and free Q&A with the teacher, teaching assistants and guest experts. Progress reports run from topic and plan in Week 13, to data and encoding in Week 14, to the quantum model in Week 15, to initial results in Week 16.
quotes: The class will include three main parts. Part One is the student report of their progress.
in Week 13 they report on the topic and a basic plan for their project.
In Week 14 one team member reports on how they ﬁnd the data and encode the data in quantum approaches.
In Week 15 another team member reports on how they set their quantum model
in Week 16 the third team member reports on some initial results
quantum computing for ETF trading, drug design or computer vision
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the organization of their own practical classes.

assertions.value: The authors state that since the autumn semester of 2021 the course has been open to global students in the Association of Pacific Rim Universities at the same time as the offline students, and that global students are undergraduates at universities such as Hong Kong University, University College London and INSA Lyon.
assertions.anchor: Jiao Tong Global Virtual Classroom, p.6
quotes: Since the autumn semester of 2021
it is open to global students in Association of Paciﬁc Rim Universities
undergraduate students in several top universities such as Hong Kong University, University College London and INSA Lyon
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the enrolment mode of their own course.

assertions.value: The authors state that the classroom was updated with four large screens and two HD webcams: three 85-inch screens on the back of the classroom and one 75-inch screen on the front-left side. One webcam captures the front of the room and tracks the teacher for a close-up of blackboard writing; the other gives a panoramic view of the class.
assertions.anchor: Jiao Tong Global Virtual Classroom, pp.6-7; Fig. 3
quotes: we have three 85-inch screens on the back of the classroom, and one 75-inch screen on the front-left side of the classroom.
additional use of four large screens and two HD webcams
it can track the teacher so that when teacher writes on the blackboard it will give the writing a close-up view automatically
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors describe the equipment of their own classroom.

assertions.value: The authors state that the blended mode needs three Zoom accounts: one for the teacher's courseware and webcam view, one connected to the front HD webcam for the panoramic view, and one controlled by the teaching assistant (TA), who is host and sets 'focus for everyone', 'replace focus video' or 'add focus video' to give close-ups of online students. They state the TA has extra work and training compared with usual classes.
assertions.anchor: Jiao Tong Global Virtual Classroom, p.7
quotes: There is extra work and training for the teaching assistant (TA) than in usual classes.
We need three Zoom accounts for the class.
In the meeting, TA is the host and teacher would be co-host if needed.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the operating procedure of their own classroom.

assertions.value: The authors claim that the classroom hardware and Zoom settings ensure effective interaction between each pair among the teacher, the offline students and the online students. The paper reports no survey, test score or other measurement of this effect.
assertions.anchor: Jiao Tong Global Virtual Classroom, p.7; Discussion, p.7
quotes: such settings for the classroom hardware and Zoom meeting ensures
that ensure a good eﬀect for international, multidisciplinary and practical studies
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim of effectiveness without evidence in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper is an experience report: it gives no learning outcome, satisfaction or comparison data for the blended mode or the practical module.

assertions.value: The authors state that all people in the course joined one WeChat discussion group, where the TA shares links to Jupyter notebooks, and claim that this works better than Canvas because it gives easier access on each person's mobile phone.
assertions.anchor: Jiao Tong Global Virtual Classroom, p.7
quotes: have joined one discussion group on Wechat
This works better than Canvas as the former provides an easier access on each’s mobilephone.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's comparison of two tools without data.

assertions.value: The authors claim that there is a huge demand in the upcoming decades for engineers and technicians who know how to use quantum sciences and technologies in their own fields, that the current workforce is largely lagging behind that target, and that the need for education on quantum sciences and technologies is severe. The paper cites no data for this.
quotes: there is a huge demand for engineers and technicians who know how to use quantum sciences and technologies in their own
the current workforce is largely lagging behind that target, and hence the
need for education on quantum sciences and technologies is severe.
assertions.certainty_reason: An unreferenced author claim about workforce demand.
assertions.reader_inference: No workforce survey, job count or forecast supports the claim in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors claim that teaching on quantum sciences and technologies is not very common even at undergraduate and graduate level, and give Shanghai Jiao Tong University, described as a top-five university in China, as an example that did not open courses on quantum computing in any department until very recent years.
quotes: the teaching for quantum sciences and technologies are not very common
has not open courses on quantum computing in any department until very recent years.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; one institution is the only example and no survey is given.
assertions.reader_inference: A single-institution example does not establish how common such teaching is.

assertions.value: The authors state that the USA signed the National Quantum Initiative Act into law and that the European Union announced a 1 billion-Euro Quantum Technologies Flagship; they cite these as examples of quantum research being emphasized at a national strategic level in many countries.
quotes: the USA signed the National Quantum Initiative Act[1] into law
announced its 1 billion-Euro Quantum Technologies Flagship[2]
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other sources (references 1 and 2).

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum sciences and technologies are generally regarded to include three main fields, quantum computing, quantum communication and quantum metrology, and that the Micius Quantum Prize followed these categories, awarded to quantum computation in 2018, quantum communication in 2019 and quantum metrology in 2020.
quotes: namely, quantum computing, quantum communication and quantum metrology
quantum computation in 2018, quantum communication in 2019, quantum metrology in 2020
assertions.certainty_reason: Background the paper attributes to a prize reference (reference 4).

assertions.value: The authors state that they were able to launch the course owing to the quick development of quantum technologies and strong demand for education, the Zhiyuan Honors Program that encourages new multidisciplinary course modules, and the strong engineering research atmosphere at the university with advice from the Academic Affairs Office.
quotes: the Zhiyuan Honors Program in the university encourages setting new innovative multidisciplinary course modules
the strong engineering research atmosphere in the university and the advice from Academic Aﬀairs Oﬃce
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own account of why the course was launched.

assertions.value: The authors state that they are writing up their teaching content on quantum computing into a tutorial book, and state as an expectation that when quantum hardware gets more mature and scalable, it may more commonly appear as a teaching tool in class.
quotes: We are writing up our teaching content on
quantum computing into a tutorial book.
when various quantum hardware get more mature and scalable, they may more commonly appear as a teaching tool in class
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of plans and an author expectation.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper treats hardware access in class as a future possibility; current teaching relies on cloud platforms and simulators.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that their efforts in curriculum development, practical module setting and blended learning make the course a case study, and they hope it can be useful for state-of-the-art education on quantum sciences and technologies.
quotes: hope this can be a useful case study for state-of-the-art education on quantum sciences and technologies.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' statement of the scope and purpose of the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The scope is a single-course experience report; it does not claim a controlled study of teaching outcomes.

papers.title_in_file: Classification and emergence of quantum spin liquids in chiral Rydberg models
papers.version_note: arXiv:2303.12829v2 (8 Aug 2023); the text layer holds the preprint once, 13 pages; figure panels and tables print as garbled text, so figure values are named in anchors only.
papers.what_it_is: A parton (projective symmetry group) classification of chiral spin liquids on the honeycomb lattice, tested against exact diagonalization and DMRG of a chiral Rydberg-atom model at 1/2 and 1/4 density.

assertions.value: The authors report a classification of fermionic chiral spin liquids with U(1) global symmetry, built by parton construction on the honeycomb lattice, that includes six distinct classes of gapped quantum spin liquids.
quotes: We classify all possible fermionic chiral spin liquids with U(1) global symmetry using parton construction on the honeycomb lattice.
The resulting classification includes six distinct classes of gapped quantum spin liquids
assertions.certainty_reason: A classification result stated in the abstract; the derivation is in Section III and Appendix B.

assertions.value: The authors state that an earlier honeycomb-lattice projective symmetry group classification finds 160 algebraic PSGs, and that without time-reversal symmetry the number of classes reduces to 24.
assertions.anchor: Section III, p.3; Appendix B, Table I, p.9
quotes: where 160 different algebraic PSG's are found.
Thus, we find that the number of different classes of algebraic PSG is reduced to 24
assertions.certainty_reason: Count of 160 is cited from Lu and Ran; the reduction to 24 is the authors' own derivation.

assertions.value: The authors state that restricting to ansatze with nonzero mean-field amplitudes on nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor links leaves 6 distinct ansatze.
quotes: Given the model that we study, we focus on those ansa¨tze that have nonzero mean-field amplitudes on the NN and NNN links. This leaves 6 distinct ansa¨tze
assertions.certainty_reason: Scope of the variational search, stated by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors state that the classification rules out a gapless Dirac spectrum, because the Dirac spin liquid submanifold preserves time-reversal symmetry, which the Hamiltonian breaks explicitly.
quotes: it rules out the possibility of gapless Dirac spectrum
However, this DSL ansatz submanifold preserves time-reversal, which is explicitly broken by our Hamiltonian.
This excludes the possibility of a DSL being stabilized in chiral systems such as our model.
assertions.certainty_reason: Argued by symmetry in the text; no formal theorem statement is given.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Wen, Wilczek and Zee, that such chiral mean-field states are stable beyond mean-field treatment because the mean-field gauge fluctuations are gapped out by the Chern-Simons mechanism.
quotes: Such chiral mean-field states are stable beyond mean-field treatment, as the mean-field gauge fluctuations are gapped out by the Chern-Simons mechanism
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (Ref. 44).

assertions.value: The authors report, from earlier work, that at small g the model is a Bose-Einstein condensate and at large g it shows spiral order, with an intermediate phase between them that shows no clear order, is believed to be a spin liquid candidate, and whose true nature remained unclear.
quotes: The intermediate phase between 0.4 ≲ g ≲ 0.9, shows no clear order, and it is believed to be a candidate for a spin liquid.
its true nature remains unclear, also due to hard-to-interpret spectral properties.
assertions.certainty_reason: Prior result from Ohler et al. (Ref. 25) restated as background.

assertions.value: The authors set up an effective hard-core boson model on the honeycomb lattice with nearest-neighbor hopping, density-assisted next-nearest-neighbor chiral hopping and nearest-neighbor interaction, with g = w2/(2µ), valid in the regime where the internal state is adiabatically eliminated and hopping is truncated at nearest-neighbor distance; the Hamiltonian has U(1) symmetry from particle-number conservation.
quotes: where J = tb and g = w2/(2µ).
The Hamiltonian has U(1) symmetry related to particle-number conservation.
Hereafter, we set the energy scale to J = 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own model in Section II.

assertions.value: The authors report that, by maximizing the overlap with the exact ground state on a 16-site cluster at g = 0.7, ansatz no. 1 has the largest overlap at 1/2 density, with amplitude ratios u2iτ0 /u1τ0 = −0.31 and u2iτ3 /uτ10 = −0.1.
quotes: The optimization is performed on a 16-site cluster at g = 0.7.
We find that the ansatz with the largest overlap with the ground state at 1/2density is ansatz no. 1
assertions.certainty_reason: A numerical optimization result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Gutzwiller-projected ansatz has a gapped mean-field state and a two-fold topological degeneracy on a torus; the overlap matrix of the four twisted-boundary states has rank 2 within a numerical accuracy on the order of 10−2.
quotes: The topological nature of such CSL is manifested by the two-fold topological degeneracy of states on a torus.
We find that the rank of the overlap matrix is 2, within a numerical accuracy on the order of 10−2.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical evidence on finite clusters.

assertions.value: The authors report a many-body Chern number C = 2 for the spinon wavefunction, computed on a D = 24 twist mesh, and divide the result by 4 because the spinon twist range corresponds to a larger twist range for the spin operators, giving a fractionalized Chern number C = 1/2 per state.
quotes: We have obtained C = 2, with the Berry curvature for D = 24 is shown in Fig. 3b.
must be divided by 4.
of the spin wavefunction is fractionalized C = 1/2 per state.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical result on one cluster.

assertions.value: The authors state that the CSL at 1/2 density is a new phase, with a dispersive single-particle band at integer filling, an interaction-driven topological phase generated from a trivial band insulator, which approaches based on flat bands would miss.
quotes: the CSL at 1/2 density is a new phase which corresponds to integer filling of the single-particle band
this CSL has a dispersive band (see Fig. 3a)
this CSL is inevitably missed by previous approaches relying on the identification of flat bands
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim of novelty.

assertions.value: The authors report that the ground-state overlap with the two topological states remains large in the intermediate phase with increasing system size, and that on a 32-site cluster the ground state is not in the rotation-neutral sector yet one of the two topological states lies in the same nontrivial rotation sector.
quotes: It can be seen that the overlap remains large in the middle phase with increasing system size
on a 32-site cluster, we find that the ground state in the intermediate phase is not in the rotation-neutral sector.
one of the two topological states is in the same nontrivial rotation sector as the ground state of the Hamiltonian
assertions.certainty_reason: Exact diagonalization on finite clusters; overlap values are in Fig. 4a only.

assertions.value: The authors report that at quarter density the CSL phase of the effective model emerges in a narrow range around g = 0.2, that ansatz no. 4 gives large overlaps, and that the overlap reaches 0.96 at the largest system size considered, L = 40.
quotes: we found that the CSL phase emerges in a narrow range around g = 0.2.
We obtain large overlaps with the ansatz no. 4 at small-size clusters in the CSL phase.
reaching 0.96 at the largest system size we considered, L = 40.
assertions.certainty_reason: Exact diagonalization overlap on finite clusters.

assertions.value: The authors report that at quarter density the approximate two-fold ground-state degeneracy is clearly visible in the ED spectra even on small clusters, and both nearly degenerate states have huge overlaps with the optimal wavefunction ansatz.
quotes: the approximate two-fold degeneracy can already be observed clearly from the ED spectra, even on small-size clusters.
both of the nearly-degenerate states have huge overlaps with the optimal wavefunction ansatz.
assertions.certainty_reason: Exact diagonalization result on small clusters.

assertions.value: The authors report that no approximate two-fold degeneracy appears in the ED spectra at half density, which they attribute to finite-size effects; at g = 0.7 the ground state has the highest overlap and one low-lying state a modest overlap, while at g = 0.1 the overlaps show no clear pattern.
assertions.anchor: Section IV, Fig. 5, p.5; Appendix C, p.10
quotes: we observe no approximate two-fold degeneracy in the ED spectra, which would have been expected in a CSL.
Nevertheless, this can be attributed to finite-size effects
at g = 0.7, we observe that the overlap is highest for the ground state, and that there is a low-lying state with a modest overlap.
at g = 0.1, the overlaps do not exhibit any clear pattern for each system size.
assertions.certainty_reason: Finite-cluster exact diagonalization; the finite-size explanation is the authors' hypothesis.
assertions.reader_inference: The missing degeneracy at 1/2 density is a weakness in the evidence for a CSL there; the paper itself leans on overlaps instead.

assertions.value: The authors report from ED on a small cluster that the gap to the first excited state may become very small at isolated twist points while the second gap and the charge gap remain wide open, which they contrast with the expected Dirac spin liquid behavior where all gaps vanish.
quotes: while the first gap may become very small at some isolated points in twist space, the second gap and charge gap remain wide open.
This contrasts with the expected behavior of a DSL, where all gaps would exhibit a vanishing behavior with respect to twist angles
assertions.certainty_reason: Exact diagonalization on finite clusters.

assertions.value: The authors propose that, for the CSL at n = 1/2 density, the two ground states lie in the same k = (0, 0) momentum sector, so their flow under flux insertion appears as an avoided crossing, which they offer as the explanation of the apparent vanishing of the first gap seen in earlier work.
quotes: In the case of CSL at n = 1/2 density, the two ground states live in the same k = (0, 0) momentum sector.
the flow between these ground states manifests as an avoided crossing.
assertions.certainty_reason: An interpretation offered by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the CSL phase at half density, even in small systems, the Kitaev-Preskill topological entanglement entropy from the exact ground state is finite and close to the value expected for a fractional quantum Hall state, and they caution that finite volume effects prevent a clear interpretation as a signature of topological order.
assertions.anchor: Section VI, Fig. 7, p.5; footnote 59, p.13
quotes: In the CSL phase, even in small systems, the computed γ is finite, and close
the finite volume effects prevent a clear interpretation of this data as a striking signature of topological order
assertions.certainty_reason: Small-cluster ED result that the authors themselves caveat.

assertions.value: The authors report from DMRG on cylinders that nearest-neighbor edge currents in the intermediate phase are significantly larger than in the neighboring phases, and that substantial counter-propagating nearest-neighbor edge currents appear only in the CSL phase and vanish in the bulk.
quotes: in the intermediate phase are significantly larger compared to those in the neighboring phases.
substantial counter-propagating NN edge currents manifests only in the CSL phase that vanish in the bulk.
assertions.certainty_reason: DMRG result on finite cylinders of periodic width 4.

assertions.value: The authors report signs of another intermediate phase with non-zero edge currents for 0.25 ≲ g ≲ 0.4 between the BEC phase and the CSL, in which reflection times time-reversal symmetry is spontaneously broken, with a two-fold degenerate ground-state manifold; they state its full characterization is beyond the scope of the work.
quotes: Notice that Fig. 1c also exhibits signatures of another intermediate phase with non-zero edge currents for 0.25 ≲ g ≲ 0.4.
While its full characterization is beyond the scope of this work
In the new intermediate phase, reflection × time-reversal symmetry gets spontaneously broken, and the total edge current becomes finite
clearly indicates two-fold degenerate ground-state manifold in this new unknown phase.
assertions.certainty_reason: Preliminary DMRG and ED findings the authors label preliminary.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the additional phase the overlap with the Dirac spin liquid wavefunction, obtained by setting the next-nearest-neighbor terms to zero, is remarkably close to the optimal overlap, and they suggest as one possible scenario that the DSL wavefunction describes the critical wavefunction at the BEC-to-new-phase transition.
quotes: Indeed, the overlap with the DSL wavefunction (blue line), which is obtained by setting the NNN interactions to zero, is remarkably close with the optimal overlap.
One possible scenario to explain this observation is that the DSL wavefunction describes the critical wavefunction at the transition from the BEC phase to the unknown phase.
assertions.certainty_reason: Overlap on one 24-site cluster; the critical-wavefunction reading is a stated possibility only.

assertions.value: The authors state that the DMRG runs use cylinders of periodic width LPBC = 4 (8 lattice sites), with MPS bond dimension in the range χ ∈ [2000, 4000] and cut-off errors of the order of 10−5 to 10−7.
quotes: periodic boundary conditions along the one axis with length LPBC = 4 (8 lattice sites)
taken in the range χ ∈ [2000, 4000] resulting in cut-off errors of the order of 10−5 to 10−7 depending on the system parameters
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own simulation setup in Appendix D.

assertions.value: The authors report that the iMPS transfer matrix spectrum shows no signature of Dirac cone behavior and is consistent with a Chern insulator, while a sharp jump in one charge sector near a twist of 0.9π may be a numerical artifact of finite bond dimension.
quotes: the results do not show any signatures of a Dirac cone behavior
the transfer matrix spectrum is consistent with a Chern insulator
we see a sharp jump in the spectrum around θPBC ≈ 0.9π which could be a numerical artifact of finite iMPS bond dimension
assertions.certainty_reason: iDMRG result at one bond dimension on one cylinder geometry.

assertions.value: The authors report from ED on periodic clusters of 24 and 28 sites that the effective model hosts a CSL regime for both truncation distances, that extending the hopping range shifts the CSL phase to the right and changes the nature of the large-g phase, and that the gap converges uniformly in g to the µ = ∞ curve as µ grows, though this is not enough to unequivocally identify a CSL at finite µ.
quotes: numerical evidence from exact diagonalization on periodic clusters of 24 and 28 sites
it shifts to the right the CSL phase and it changes the nature of the large-g phase
We observe convergence (uniformly in g) to the µ = ∞ curve
to unequivocally identify a CSL phase at finite
assertions.certainty_reason: ED on small clusters, reported with an explicit caveat.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Appendix A analysis only probes the validity of the adiabatic elimination at different hopping truncations, and does not probe the stability of a CSL phase at finite µ and longer hopping range in a generic filling sector.
quotes: does not aim at probing the stability of a CSL phase at finite µ and RT > 1 in a generic filling sector.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its own scope in Appendix A.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that Gutzwiller-projected parton CSL wavefunctions capture the intermediate disordered phase in chiral Rydberg atom arrays and resolve the previously unclear nature of the intermediate phase found in Ref. 25.
quotes: We show that the CSL wavefunctions constructed from the Gutzwiller-projected parton wavefunctions are able to capture the intermediate disordered phase in chiral Rydberg atom arrays.
our results resolve the previously unclear nature of the intermediate phase found in Ref. [25].
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion, resting on finite-cluster evidence.
assertions.reader_inference: The text elsewhere admits missing two-fold degeneracy at 1/2 density and finite-size caveats on entanglement entropy, so resolve is stronger than the evidence shown.

papers.title_in_file: Study Finds Exponential Quantum Advantage in Machine Learning Tasks
papers.version_note: A news article by Matt Swayne in The Quantum Insider, dated April 10, 2026 (page header shows September 24, 2026, the capture date). It reports on an arXiv preprint; it is not the preprint. The text holds no page breaks, so it is one page.
papers.what_it_is: A trade-press news report on an arXiv preprint (Caltech, Google Quantum AI, MIT, Oratomic) claiming a memory-based exponential quantum advantage for classification, dimension reduction and linear system solving via quantum oracle sketching.

assertions.value: The article reports that the study introduces a method called quantum oracle sketching, in which the quantum computer ingests data samples one at a time, applies a sequence of small quantum operations and discards each sample, so the full dataset is never stored.
quotes: The new study introduces a method called "quantum oracle sketching," which allows a quantum computer to process data streams without storing the full dataset.
the system ingests samples one at a time, applies a sequence of small quantum operations and discards each sample after processing.
assertions.certainty_reason: A journalist's description of a preprint's method; the preprint itself is not read here.

assertions.value: The article states that the oracle sketching method replaces earlier approaches that relied on quantum random access memory (QRAM), which would require complex and resource-intensive hardware.
quotes: The method replaces earlier approaches that relied on quantum random access memory, or QRAM, which would require complex and resource-intensive hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: Secondary report of the authors' framing.
assertions.reader_inference: The article says the method replaces QRAM-based loading; whether it does so for every QRAM-based algorithm is not shown in the article.

assertions.value: The article reports that the researchers combine the data-loading method with classical shadow tomography, so that the system can produce classical outputs such as trained models without reconstructing or storing the entire dataset.
quotes: The researchers combine this data-loading method with a second technique known as classical shadow tomography.
the techniques allow the system to produce classical outputs — such as trained models — without needing to reconstruct or store the entire dataset.
assertions.certainty_reason: Secondary report of a preprint's method.

assertions.value: The article reports that, in simulations on movie review sentiment analysis and single-cell RNA sequencing datasets, the quantum approach achieved performance comparable to classical methods with a memory reduction of four to six orders of magnitude, using fewer than 60 logical qubits.
quotes: The study reports simulation results on real-world datasets, including movie review sentiment analysis and single-cell RNA sequencing.
the memory reduction ranged from four to six orders of magnitude, with the quantum system operating with fewer than 60 logical qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical (simulated) result reported second hand from a preprint.

assertions.value: The article states that the memory-reduction results are based on simulations and theoretical analysis rather than experiments on physical quantum hardware.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Preserving Quantum Advantages', paragraph 4, and 'Still at The Theoretical Stage', p.1
quotes: Important to note: That's based on simulations and theoretical analysis rather than experiments on physical quantum hardware.
The experiments are based on numerical simulations rather than physical quantum hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: The article states this limit of the study's evidence in its own words, twice.

assertions.value: The article states that the study defines quantum advantage in terms of memory rather than speed: quantum systems may require far less storage to perform the same tasks.
quotes: Much of the field has focused on speed
This study instead emphasizes memory, showing that quantum systems may require far less storage to perform the same tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author's framing relayed by a journalist.

assertions.value: The article reports that the researchers show, for the types of tasks considered, that any classical system matching the quantum system's performance would need exponentially more memory or significantly more data samples, and that this separation holds even with unlimited classical time.
quotes: any classical system that matches the quantum system's performance would need exponentially more memory or significantly more data samples.
This separation holds even if classical systems are given unlimited time
assertions.certainty_reason: The article gives no theorem statement or conditions; the proof is in the preprint, which is not read here.
assertions.reader_inference: The article quotes no theorem statement, so the exact conditions of the separation (data model, accuracy, constants) are not available from this source.

assertions.value: The article states that the work focuses on three core applications: solving large systems of equations, classification, and dimension reduction.
quotes: The work focuses on three core applications.
The second is classification
The third is dimension reduction
assertions.certainty_reason: The article states the scope of the study in its own words.

assertions.value: The article reports that, in each case, a quantum system with a number of qubits that grows slowly with problem size can complete the task using a manageable number of data samples, whereas classical systems face a trade-off between memory and accuracy, particularly with streaming methods.
quotes: a quantum system with a number of qubits that grows slowly with problem size can complete the task using a manageable number of data samples.
Classical systems, by contrast, face a trade-off between memory and accuracy
assertions.certainty_reason: Second-hand statement without the scaling laws.
assertions.reader_inference: The article gives no explicit qubit or sample scaling, so the claim cannot be checked against it.

assertions.value: The article reports that, for data that changes over time, the study indicates classical systems require far more data samples to keep up while quantum systems maintain efficiency.
quotes: classical systems require far more data samples to keep up, while quantum systems maintain efficiency.
assertions.certainty_reason: Second-hand statement; the article adds that this suggests a potential advantage.

assertions.value: The article states that current quantum computers are limited by noise, error rates and the difficulty of maintaining stable qubits, and that scaling from tens of logical qubits to the hundreds or more needed for practical deployment remains a significant challenge.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Still at The Theoretical Stage', paragraph 1, p.1
quotes: Current quantum computers are limited by noise, error rates and the difficulty of maintaining stable qubits.
Scaling from tens of logical qubits to the hundreds or more needed for practical deployment remains a significant challenge.
assertions.certainty_reason: The article states this limit in its own words.

assertions.value: The article states that the study assumes certain ideal conditions, such as reliable access to data samples and well-behaved datasets, and that experimental validation will be needed to confirm performance at scale.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Still at The Theoretical Stage', paragraph 2, p.1
quotes: The study also assumes certain ideal conditions, such as reliable access to data samples and well-behaved datasets.
experimental validation will be needed to confirm performance at scale.
assertions.certainty_reason: The article states the study's assumptions and the need for validation.

assertions.value: The article states that the quantum method still requires processing a large number of data samples, that the data-loading step dominates the runtime, and that the researchers say this is unlikely to be significantly reduced without further advances.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Still at The Theoretical Stage', paragraph 3, p.1
quotes: The quantum method still requires processing a large number of data samples
the data-loading step dominates the runtime and is unlikely to be significantly reduced without further advances.
assertions.certainty_reason: A limit of the result stated in the article.
assertions.reader_inference: The advantage is in memory, not runtime, per the article's own account.

assertions.value: The article states that integrating quantum components into data-processing pipelines, which mostly rely on distributed classical infrastructure, will require new software tools and system designs.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Still at The Theoretical Stage', paragraph 4, p.1
quotes: Most data-processing pipelines rely on distributed classical infrastructure.
will require new software tools and system designs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The journalist's assessment, without evidence in the article.

assertions.value: The article states that the study outlines future work on hybrid quantum-classical systems, on further applications including optimization, signal processing and scientific simulations, and on experimental validation on real quantum hardware.
quotes: One area is the development of hybrid systems that combine quantum and classical methods
including optimization, signal processing and scientific simulations
Demonstrating these effects on real quantum hardware would provide stronger evidence for the claimed advantages
assertions.certainty_reason: The article states the open directions and the lack of hardware evidence.

assertions.value: The article lists the research team as Haimeng Zhao and Hsin-Yuan Huang of Caltech, Alexander Zlokapa of MIT, Hartmut Neven, Ryan Babbush and Jarrod R. McClean of Google Quantum AI, and John Preskill of Caltech and Oratomic, and states that the study is an arXiv pre-print that is not peer reviewed.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Future Work', last two paragraphs, p.1
quotes: Haimeng Zhao and Hsin-Yuan Huang of the California Institute of Technology
Alexander Zlokapa of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology
arXiv is a pre-print server
it is not — nor is this article, itself — official peer-review publications.
assertions.certainty_reason: The article states authorship and the preprint status of its subject directly.
assertions.reader_inference: The article names no arXiv identifier; the underlying preprint must be located separately before its claims are entered.
